questions.stem: Which statement best defines an independent clause?

options.text: A word group with a subject and a verb that cannot stand alone and must attach to another clause
A word group with a subject and a finite verb that expresses a complete thought and can stand alone
A word group beginning with a preposition that adds detail about place, time, or manner
A word group containing a verb form but no subject, used to modify a noun in the sentence

rationales.whyCorrect: An independent (main) clause has both a subject and a finite verb and conveys a complete thought, so it can function alone as a simple sentence. Choice A describes a dependent (subordinate) clause, which is typically introduced by a dependent marker word such as because, although, or when; choice C describes a prepositional phrase; choice D describes a participial phrase. Because a phrase has no subject-verb pair, only clauses can be classified as independent or dependent, and that distinction is the basis for recognizing fragments and run-ons in clinical documentation.
rationales.eli10: Use a two-part test on any word group. First, is there someone or something doing something (subject plus a verb that shows tense)? Second, if you said it aloud and stopped, would the listener be satisfied? 'The patient rested' passes both. 'Because the patient rested' passes the first but fails the second, because 'because' promises more information. 'During the night shift' fails the first test entirely, since there is no subject or verb at all.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: An independent (main) clause has both a subject and a finite verb and conveys a complete thought, so it can function alone as a simple sentence. Choice A describes a dependent (subordinate) clause, which is typically introduced by a dependent marker word such as because, although, or when; choice C describes a prepositional phrase; choice D describes a participial phrase. Because a phrase has no subject-verb pair, only clauses can be classified as independent or dependent, and that distinction is the basis for recognizing fragments and run-ons in clinical documentation.

questions.stem: Which example is a sentence fragment rather than a complete sentence?

options.text: The nurse charted the vital signs.
Report the findings immediately.
Hydration improved after the second liter of fluid.
Although the wound appeared clean at the morning assessment.

rationales.whyCorrect: Choice D contains a subject and a verb but is introduced by the subordinating conjunction 'although,' which makes the clause dependent and leaves the thought unresolved; it must be attached to an independent clause. Choices A and C are complete simple sentences, and choice B is an imperative, which is complete because its subject 'you' is understood rather than missing. Scanning for dependent marker words at the start of a word group is the quickest proofreading check for this error.
rationales.eli10: Words such as although, because, when, since, and if act as flags: whatever follows them is only half of the message. Read choice D aloud and your mind waits for the second half, and that unresolved feeling is exactly what a fragment is. Commands feel different, because 'Report the findings' already gives you the whole instruction; the subject 'you' is understood rather than absent, so nothing is left hanging.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Choice D contains a subject and a verb but is introduced by the subordinating conjunction 'although,' which makes the clause dependent and leaves the thought unresolved; it must be attached to an independent clause. Choices A and C are complete simple sentences, and choice B is an imperative, which is complete because its subject 'you' is understood rather than missing. Scanning for dependent marker words at the start of a word group is the quickest proofreading check for this error.

questions.stem: What is the defining feature of a compound sentence?

options.text: It contains two or more independent clauses and no dependent clause.
It contains one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.
It contains at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause.
It contains one independent clause expanded by several modifying phrases.

rationales.whyCorrect: A compound sentence joins two or more independent clauses using a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, a semicolon, or a semicolon followed by a conjunctive adverb; by definition it contains no dependent clause. Choice B defines a complex sentence, choice C defines a compound-complex sentence, and choice D defines a simple sentence, since phrases do not add clauses. Classifying by clause count rather than by sentence length is what makes the four sentence types usable in practice.
rationales.eli10: Classify by counting, not by feel. Find every subject-verb pair, then ask which pairs could survive on their own. Two or more survivors and no leaners equals compound. Add a leaner such as 'because the census was high' and it becomes compound-complex. A long sentence can still be simple: 'The charge nurse reviewed the assignments for the entire night shift' has one subject-verb pair, so length changes nothing.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: A compound sentence joins two or more independent clauses using a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, a semicolon, or a semicolon followed by a conjunctive adverb; by definition it contains no dependent clause. Choice B defines a complex sentence, choice C defines a compound-complex sentence, and choice D defines a simple sentence, since phrases do not add clauses. Classifying by clause count rather than by sentence length is what makes the four sentence types usable in practice.

questions.stem: Why does joining two independent clauses with only a comma create an error?

options.text: A comma may never appear between the two verbs of a single sentence.
A comma marks a pause but cannot join two complete thoughts, so a comma splice results.
A comma shifts the tense relationship between clauses and blurs the sequence of events.
A comma may follow only a dependent clause and never an independent clause.

rationales.whyCorrect: A comma separates elements within a sentence but has no clause-joining force; linking two independent clauses requires a coordinating conjunction after the comma, a semicolon, a colon, or a period. Using a comma alone produces a comma splice, which Purdue OWL lists alongside fused sentences as a primary run-on error. Choices A, C, and D misstate comma function: commas do routinely follow independent clauses before a coordinating conjunction, and they carry no tense meaning at all.
rationales.eli10: Think about the workload each mark can carry. A comma handles small separations inside one sentence, such as items in a list or an introductory element. Two complete statements meeting is a much heavier job, so it needs a stronger connector. 'The IV infiltrated, the nurse stopped the infusion' overloads the comma. Add 'and' after it, upgrade to a semicolon, or split into two sentences, and the load is carried properly.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: A comma separates elements within a sentence but has no clause-joining force; linking two independent clauses requires a coordinating conjunction after the comma, a semicolon, a colon, or a period. Using a comma alone produces a comma splice, which Purdue OWL lists alongside fused sentences as a primary run-on error. Choices A, C, and D misstate comma function: commas do routinely follow independent clauses before a coordinating conjunction, and they carry no tense meaning at all.

questions.stem: Which comparison of coordinating and subordinating conjunctions is accurate?

options.text: Coordinating conjunctions join grammatically equal elements, while subordinating conjunctions make one clause dependent.
Coordinating conjunctions rank one idea above the other, while subordinating conjunctions treat both as equal.
Both types create dependent clauses, but only subordinating conjunctions require a preceding comma.
Coordinating conjunctions may join only whole clauses, while subordinating conjunctions may join only single words.

rationales.whyCorrect: The seven coordinating conjunctions (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) link elements of equal grammatical rank, whether words, phrases, or independent clauses. Subordinating conjunctions such as because, although, while, since, if, when, and after convert an independent clause into a dependent one and specify a relationship of cause, contrast, time, or condition. Choice B reverses the two definitions; choice C is false because coordinators never create dependency; choice D is false because coordinators can join words and phrases, not only clauses.
rationales.eli10: Test the effect of the word on the clause behind it. Put 'and' in front of 'the students practiced' and the clause is unchanged; it could still stand alone once the 'and' is removed. Put 'because' in front and the clause immediately needs a partner. That is the whole difference: coordinators connect without changing status, while subordinators demote one clause into supporting information for another.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: The seven coordinating conjunctions (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) link elements of equal grammatical rank, whether words, phrases, or independent clauses. Subordinating conjunctions such as because, although, while, since, if, when, and after convert an independent clause into a dependent one and specify a relationship of cause, contrast, time, or condition. Choice B reverses the two definitions; choice C is false because coordinators never create dependency; choice D is false because coordinators can join words and phrases, not only clauses.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of subordination in sentence construction?

options.text: To shorten sentences by deleting verbs that repeat information already stated
To keep every sentence in a paragraph at approximately the same length
To show the logical relationship between ideas and mark which idea carries the emphasis
To replace punctuation so that commas and semicolons become unnecessary

rationales.whyCorrect: Subordination names the relationship between two ideas, such as cause, time, condition, or contrast, and places the writer's main point in the independent clause. Compare 'The patient ambulated, and she reported dizziness' with 'When the patient ambulated, she reported dizziness': the second version fixes the timing and foregrounds the symptom. Choice A describes ellipsis, choice B describes an undesirable monotony rather than a goal, and choice D is backward, since a fronted dependent clause normally adds a comma requirement.
rationales.eli10: Subordination is how you tell a reader what matters most. Both facts remain, but only one sits in the independent clause, and that is the one the reader carries away. Flip the structure and you flip the emphasis: 'Although her pain improved, she remained febrile' leaves the reader thinking about the fever, while 'Although she remained febrile, her pain improved' leaves them thinking about the improvement. Same two facts, different message.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Subordination names the relationship between two ideas, such as cause, time, condition, or contrast, and places the writer's main point in the independent clause. Compare 'The patient ambulated, and she reported dizziness' with 'When the patient ambulated, she reported dizziness': the second version fixes the timing and foregrounds the symptom. Choice A describes ellipsis, choice B describes an undesirable monotony rather than a goal, and choice D is backward, since a fronted dependent clause normally adds a comma requirement.

questions.stem: What would happen if the subordinating conjunction were deleted from 'Because the medication was delayed, the pain score increased'?

options.text: Both clauses would become independent, so the comma alone would create a comma splice.
The first clause would lose its verb, leaving the sentence a fragment.
The sentence would remain complex, and the causal relationship would still be stated explicitly.
The sentence would stay correct but would be reclassified as compound-complex.

rationales.whyCorrect: Deleting 'because' restores 'the medication was delayed' to independent status, and a comma can no longer join it to the second independent clause; the result, 'The medication was delayed, the pain score increased,' is a comma splice. The explicit causal link disappears as well, leaving the reader to infer it. Repair requires a comma plus 'so,' a semicolon, or a period, which demonstrates that a single subordinator governs both punctuation and meaning.
rationales.eli10: 'Because' is doing two jobs at once. It states the causal relationship, and it lowers the first clause to dependent status, which is what makes a single comma sufficient. Remove it and the first clause is promoted back to a full sentence, so the punctuation that was correct a moment ago is now too weak. Whenever you delete or add a subordinator, recheck the comma, because the two decisions are linked.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Deleting 'because' restores 'the medication was delayed' to independent status, and a comma can no longer join it to the second independent clause; the result, 'The medication was delayed, the pain score increased,' is a comma splice. The explicit causal link disappears as well, leaving the reader to infer it. Repair requires a comma plus 'so,' a semicolon, or a period, which demonstrates that a single subordinator governs both punctuation and meaning.

questions.stem: Which revision best corrects the run-on 'The client refused the morning dose he stated it caused nausea'?

options.text: The client refused the morning dose, he stated it caused nausea.
The client refused the morning dose he stated, it caused nausea.
The client refused the morning dose; because he stated it caused nausea.
The client refused the morning dose; he stated it caused nausea.

rationales.whyCorrect: The original is a fused sentence: two independent clauses run together with no punctuation. A semicolon is the correct repair because it joins two closely related independent clauses without adding a relationship the record does not document. Choice A downgrades the fused sentence to a comma splice, choice C misuses a semicolon before a dependent clause (a semicolon requires an independent clause on each side), and choice B moves commas around without addressing the clause junction.
rationales.eli10: First locate the seam. Read forward until you reach a point where a complete sentence has just ended; here that is after 'dose.' Then choose a connector strong enough for two full statements: a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. A comma by itself is too weak, which rules out choice A. A semicolon followed by 'because' fails for the opposite reason, since 'because he stated it caused nausea' cannot stand alone, and a semicolon needs a full sentence on both sides.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: The original is a fused sentence: two independent clauses run together with no punctuation. A semicolon is the correct repair because it joins two closely related independent clauses without adding a relationship the record does not document. Choice A downgrades the fused sentence to a comma splice, choice C misuses a semicolon before a dependent clause (a semicolon requires an independent clause on each side), and choice B moves commas around without addressing the clause junction.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly classified as complex?

options.text: The instructor demonstrated the procedure, and the students practiced it twice.
After the instructor demonstrated the procedure, the students practiced it twice.
The instructor demonstrated the procedure during the afternoon skills lab session.
The instructor demonstrated the procedure; the students practiced it twice.

rationales.whyCorrect: A complex sentence contains one independent clause plus at least one dependent clause, which choice B achieves with the introductory clause beginning with the dependent marker 'after.' Choices A and D are compound, joined by a comma plus a coordinating conjunction and by a semicolon respectively; choice C is simple, since 'during the afternoon skills lab session' is a prepositional phrase with no subject-verb pair. Note also that the fronted dependent clause takes a comma, whereas the same clause placed at the end ordinarily would not.
rationales.eli10: Work through it mechanically. Count the subject-verb pairs, then mark which ones could stand alone. In choice B, 'the students practiced it twice' stands alone, but 'After the instructor demonstrated the procedure' cannot, so you have one independent plus one dependent, which is complex. Choice C has extra words but only one subject-verb pair, a reminder that added phrases lengthen a sentence without changing its type.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: A complex sentence contains one independent clause plus at least one dependent clause, which choice B achieves with the introductory clause beginning with the dependent marker 'after.' Choices A and D are compound, joined by a comma plus a coordinating conjunction and by a semicolon respectively; choice C is simple, since 'during the afternoon skills lab session' is a prepositional phrase with no subject-verb pair. Note also that the fronted dependent clause takes a comma, whereas the same clause placed at the end ordinarily would not.

questions.stem: Which change would most likely improve the choppy passage 'The patient was admitted at noon. The patient was febrile. The patient received acetaminophen.'?

options.text: Replace each period with a comma so the three statements run together as one continuous idea.
Reverse the order of the three sentences so the treatment is reported before the assessment findings.
Combine the ideas through subordination, as in 'The patient, who was febrile on admission at noon, received acetaminophen.'
Begin each of the three sentences with a different transitional adverb so the statements sound connected.

rationales.whyCorrect: Sentence combining folds the supporting details into a subordinate structure, here a nonrestrictive relative clause, so the intervention occupies the independent clause and receives the emphasis. Choice A produces comma splices rather than a legitimate join; choice B reverses the chronology and misrepresents the sequence of care; choice D leaves three short repetitive clauses intact and risks asserting logical relationships (contrast, result) that the original facts do not establish. Varying structure improves readability without altering the clinical content.
rationales.eli10: Three sentences that all start with the same subject signal that they belong in one sentence. Decide which fact is the point, since that one keeps the independent clause; here it is the medication. The other two facts are background about the patient, so they can slide into a 'who' clause. The test for the result is whether removing the tucked-in part still leaves a working sentence: 'The patient received acetaminophen' works, so the combining was done correctly.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Sentence combining folds the supporting details into a subordinate structure, here a nonrestrictive relative clause, so the intervention occupies the independent clause and receives the emphasis. Choice A produces comma splices rather than a legitimate join; choice B reverses the chronology and misrepresents the sequence of care; choice D leaves three short repetitive clauses intact and risks asserting logical relationships (contrast, result) that the original facts do not establish. Varying structure improves readability without altering the clinical content.

questions.stem: Which sentence demonstrates compound-complex structure with correct punctuation?

options.text: Although the shift was short, the unit stayed unusually busy.
Because the shift was short and the unit stayed busy, the charting piled up.
The shift was short, although the unit stayed busy, the charting piled up.
Although the shift was short, the unit stayed busy, and the charting piled up.

rationales.whyCorrect: Choice D contains one dependent clause ('Although the shift was short') plus two independent clauses joined by a comma and the coordinating conjunction 'and,' which is precisely the compound-complex pattern with standard punctuation. Choice A is complex, with one dependent and one independent clause. Choice B is also complex, because the 'and' joins two clauses inside the single 'because' structure, leaving only one independent clause. Choice C strings clauses together with commas only, producing a comma splice.
rationales.eli10: Compound-complex requires two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause, so count both categories rather than counting clauses in total. Choice B is the trap: it has three subject-verb pairs, which looks like enough, but 'because' reaches across the 'and' and covers both of the first two clauses, so both lean and only one clause stands alone. Test it by reading each clause in isolation and asking whether it could be a sentence on its own.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Choice D contains one dependent clause ('Although the shift was short') plus two independent clauses joined by a comma and the coordinating conjunction 'and,' which is precisely the compound-complex pattern with standard punctuation. Choice A is complex, with one dependent and one independent clause. Choice B is also complex, because the 'and' joins two clauses inside the single 'because' structure, leaving only one independent clause. questions.stem: A student writes: 'The dressing was saturated, however, the site showed no active bleeding.' Which explanation of the error is accurate?

options.text: 'However' may appear only at the beginning of a sentence, so its position in the middle is the error.
'However' is a subordinating conjunction, so the first clause is now dependent and the sentence is a fragment.
'However' is a conjunctive adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so a semicolon or period must precede it.
'However' functions like 'but,' so the comma before it correctly joins the two independent clauses.

rationales.whyCorrect: Conjunctive adverbs such as however, therefore, moreover, and consequently signal logical relationships but have no clause-joining power, so a comma before one leaves a comma splice. The accepted forms are 'The dressing was saturated; however, the site showed no active bleeding' or two sentences with 'However,' opening the second. Choice B misidentifies the word class, choice A invents a placement rule that does not exist, and choice D repeats the very misconception that produces the error, since only the seven coordinating conjunctions can join independent clauses after a comma.
rationales.eli10: Compare 'however' with 'but' by trying to move each one. 'But' is locked in place between the two clauses, which is what a real joining word does. 'However' can slide: 'the site, however, showed no active bleeding' still works, because it is an adverb commenting on the clause rather than binding two clauses together. Anything that can move like that cannot be carrying the join, so the semicolon or period has to do that work instead.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Conjunctive adverbs such as however, therefore, moreover, and consequently signal logical relationships but have no clause-joining power, so a comma before one leaves a comma splice. The accepted forms are 'The dressing was saturated; however, the site showed no active bleeding' or two sentences with 'However,' opening the second. Choice B misidentifies the word class, choice A invents a placement rule that does not exist, and choice D repeats the very misconception that produces the error, since only the seven coordinating conjunctions can join independent clauses after a comma.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines subject-verb agreement?

options.text: A verb must be placed immediately after its subject in every complete sentence
A verb must agree in number with whichever noun stands closest to it
A verb must match the tense of any modifier that describes the subject
A verb must agree with its grammatical subject in number and in person

rationales.whyCorrect: Subject-verb agreement is a rule of grammatical concord: a singular subject takes a singular verb form and a plural subject takes a plural verb form, and the verb also reflects person (first, second, third), as in 'I am,' 'she is,' 'they are.' Agreement is controlled by the grammatical subject, not by word order (choice A), not by the nearest noun (choice B), and not by tense relationships with modifiers (choice C). In clinical documentation, agreement errors blur who or what performed an action, which undermines the precision a chart entry requires.
rationales.eli10: Think of a subject and its verb as dance partners who must step together. One person dancing alone takes the solo step: 'The nurse checks.' A whole group takes the group step: 'The nurses check.' Person matters too, which is why 'I am' and 'she is' use different forms of the same verb. Other nouns hanging around the sentence do not get a vote; only the actual subject decides the verb's step.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Subject-verb agreement is a rule of grammatical concord: a singular subject takes a singular verb form and a plural subject takes a plural verb form, and the verb also reflects person (first, second, third), as in 'I am,' 'she is,' 'they are.' Agreement is controlled by the grammatical subject, not by word order (choice A), not by the nearest noun (choice B), and not by tense relationships with modifiers (choice C). In clinical documentation, agreement errors blur who or what performed an action, which undermines the precision a chart entry requires.

questions.stem: Which description best identifies an independent clause?

options.text: A word group with a subject and predicate introduced by a subordinating conjunction
A word group built around a nonfinite verb form such as a participle or an infinitive
A word group with a subject and a predicate that can stand alone as a sentence
A word group with no subject that modifies a noun and adds descriptive detail

rationales.whyCorrect: An independent (main) clause contains a subject and a finite predicate and expresses a complete thought, so it can function alone as a sentence. Choice A describes a dependent (subordinate) clause, which has a subject and predicate but is subordinated by a word such as 'because' or 'although'; choice B describes a verbal phrase, which is nonfinite and forms no clause; choice D describes a modifying phrase. Identifying independent clauses is the prerequisite for punctuating compound sentences and for recognizing fragments and comma splices.
rationales.eli10: An independent clause is like a person who can live alone: it has someone doing something (the subject) and the doing itself (a finite verb). 'The patient rested.' That is a whole sentence. Put 'because' in front and it suddenly needs a roommate: 'Because the patient rested...' leaves the reader waiting. Note that the subject and verb are still there; the subordinating word is what makes the clause dependent rather than independent.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: An independent (main) clause contains a subject and a finite predicate and expresses a complete thought, so it can function alone as a sentence. Choice A describes a dependent (subordinate) clause, which has a subject and predicate but is subordinated by a word such as 'because' or 'although'; choice B describes a verbal phrase, which is nonfinite and forms no clause; choice D describes a modifying phrase. Identifying independent clauses is the prerequisite for punctuating compound sentences and for recognizing fragments and comma splices.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The patient reported that his pain had worsened,' what grammatical term names the word 'patient' in relation to the pronoun 'his'?

options.text: The antecedent
The predicate nominative
The direct object
The appositive

rationales.whyCorrect: An antecedent is the noun or noun phrase that a pronoun refers back to; here the possessive pronoun 'his' refers to 'patient.' An appositive is a noun placed beside another noun to rename it, a predicate nominative renames the subject after a linking verb, and a direct object receives the action of a transitive verb, so none of those terms describes this relationship. The term matters because pronouns with missing, distant, or ambiguous antecedents are a leading source of unclear writing.
rationales.eli10: A pronoun works like a shortcut arrow pointing backward. When a reader hits 'his,' the mind flips back to find who is meant and lands on 'patient.' The word the arrow lands on is the antecedent, from Latin roots meaning 'going before.' The trouble starts when the arrow points at nothing, or at two possible people, as in 'The nurse told the patient that she was late' -- the reader cannot tell who 'she' is.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: An antecedent is the noun or noun phrase that a pronoun refers back to; here the possessive pronoun 'his' refers to 'patient.' An appositive is a noun placed beside another noun to rename it, a predicate nominative renames the subject after a linking verb, and a direct object receives the action of a transitive verb, so none of those terms describes this relationship. The term matters because pronouns with missing, distant, or ambiguous antecedents are a leading source of unclear writing.

questions.stem: Why does the sentence 'The patient reported nausea, the nurse documented the symptom' require revision?

options.text: It is a sentence fragment, because neither word group expresses a complete thought
It is a fused sentence, because two independent clauses run together with no punctuation
It is a comma splice, because two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone
It shows faulty parallelism, because the two clauses use mismatched verb forms

rationales.whyCorrect: Each word group has a subject and a finite verb and could stand alone, so a comma by itself is too weak a mark to join them. Standard repairs include a period, a semicolon, a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (and, but, so), or subordination of one clause ('After the patient reported nausea, the nurse documented the symptom'). Choice B names the closely related error in which clauses are run together with no punctuation at all, which is not what appears here.
rationales.eli10: A comma is a speed bump, not a stop sign. Two complete sentences meeting each other need something stronger: a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a joining word like 'and.' When only the speed bump is used, the sentences slide into each other, and that slide is a comma splice. The related error with no mark at all is a fused or run-on sentence; both are fixed by choosing a bigger traffic signal.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Each word group has a subject and a finite verb and could stand alone, so a comma by itself is too weak a mark to join them. Standard repairs include a period, a semicolon, a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (and, but, so), or subordination of one clause ('After the patient reported nausea, the nurse documented the symptom'). Choice B names the closely related error in which clauses are run together with no punctuation at all, which is not what appears here.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains the grammatical problem in 'While charting the assessment, the call light rang'?

options.text: The sentence is a fragment, because the introductory word group contains no finite verb
The introductory modifier has no logical subject in the clause it modifies, so it describes the call light
The verb tense shifts illogically from the introductory word group to the main clause
The two clauses are joined without a coordinating conjunction, producing a run-on sentence

rationales.whyCorrect: An introductory modifier of this kind, an elliptical clause whose subject has been omitted before the -ing verb, is understood to attach to the subject of the main clause. Because that subject is 'the call light,' the sentence literally states that the call light was charting, the classic dangling modifier. Choice A is wrong because the sentence as a whole has a subject and a finite verb ('rang'); choice D misdescribes the structure, since only one independent clause is present. Repair it by supplying the missing actor as the subject ('While charting the assessment, I heard the call light ring') or by expanding the phrase into a full clause ('While I was charting the assessment, the call light rang').
rationales.eli10: An opening word group like 'While charting the assessment' never names its own doer, so English assigns it the subject of the clause that follows the comma. Here that subject is 'the call light,' so the sentence claims a plastic device was doing paperwork. The modifier is left dangling with nothing sensible to attach to. The fix is either to put the real actor right after the comma or to write the doer into the opening group itself.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: An introductory modifier of this kind, an elliptical clause whose subject has been omitted before the -ing verb, is understood to attach to the subject of the main clause. Because that subject is 'the call light,' the sentence literally states that the call light was charting, the classic dangling modifier. Choice A is wrong because the sentence as a whole has a subject and a finite verb ('rang'); choice D misdescribes the structure, since only one independent clause is present. Repair it by supplying the missing actor as the subject ('While charting the assessment, I heard the call light ring') or by expanding the phrase into a full clause ('While I was charting the assessment, the call light rang').

questions.stem: Which comparison of active and passive voice is accurate?

options.text: Active voice makes the actor the grammatical subject, while passive voice is appropriate when the actor is unknown or unimportant
Active voice is required in formal writing, while passive voice is a grammatical error that careful editors remove on sight
Active voice belongs to present-tense writing, while passive voice belongs to past-tense writing about completed events
Passive voice is signaled by any appearance of a form of 'to be,' while active voice never uses auxiliary verbs

rationales.whyCorrect: Voice describes the relationship between the subject and the action: in active voice the subject performs the action, and in the passive (a form of 'be' plus a past participle) the subject receives it. Passive constructions are fully grammatical and are conventional when the agent is unknown, obvious, or irrelevant, as in methods sections of scientific writing. Voice is independent of tense, so choice C fails, and a form of 'to be' alone does not mark the passive, since progressive ('she is charting') and linking ('she is tired') constructions also use it.
rationales.eli10: Active voice puts the doer in the driver's seat: 'The nurse gave the medication.' Passive moves the doer to the back seat or leaves them out entirely: 'The medication was given.' Neither is against the rules. Passive helps when nobody knows who acted, or when the thing done matters more than the person who did it. But when accountability is the point, put the driver back behind the wheel so the reader knows exactly who acted.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Voice describes the relationship between the subject and the action: in active voice the subject performs the action, and in the passive (a form of 'be' plus a past participle) the subject receives it. Passive constructions are fully grammatical and are conventional when the agent is unknown, obvious, or irrelevant, as in methods sections of scientific writing. Voice is independent of tense, so choice C fails, and a form of 'to be' alone does not mark the passive, since progressive ('she is charting') and linking ('she is tired') constructions also use it.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'Each of the nurses ___ responsible for verifying the count,' which explanation identifies the correct verb form?

options.text: 'are,' because the plural noun 'nurses' stands immediately before the verb slot
'are,' because the expression 'each of' refers collectively to more than one person
'is,' because a verb that follows an intervening prepositional phrase is always singular
'is,' because the subject is 'each,' and 'of the nurses' is a prepositional phrase

rationales.whyCorrect: The simple subject is the singular indefinite pronoun 'each,' and 'of the nurses' is an intervening prepositional phrase; the object of a preposition can never serve as the subject of the sentence. Nearness to a plural noun produces the common error called agreement by attraction, but agreement is determined structurally rather than by proximity. Choice C states a rule that does not exist: in 'A number of the nurses are available,' an intervening phrase is present and the verb is still plural.
rationales.eli10: Cover the words between the subject and the verb with your thumb and reread: 'Each ___ responsible.' The ear immediately supplies 'is.' The phrase 'of the nurses' is scenery along the way, and scenery does not get to control the verb. 'Each' means one at a time, so it stays singular no matter how large the group it selects from. The same test works for 'either,' 'neither,' and 'one of.'
rationales.distractorAnalysis: The simple subject is the singular indefinite pronoun 'each,' and 'of the nurses' is an intervening prepositional phrase; the object of a preposition can never serve as the subject of the sentence. Nearness to a plural noun produces the common error called agreement by attraction, but agreement is determined structurally rather than by proximity. questions.stem: Which sentence punctuates the conjunctive adverb correctly?

options.text: The patient's vital signs were stable, however, she reported new dizziness.
The patient's vital signs were stable, however; she reported new dizziness.
The patient's vital signs were stable however; she reported new dizziness.
The patient's vital signs were stable; however, she reported new dizziness.

rationales.whyCorrect: 'However' is a conjunctive adverb rather than a coordinating conjunction, so it cannot join two independent clauses with a comma alone; a semicolon (or a period) must fall at the clause boundary, and a comma normally follows the adverb. Choice A is therefore a comma splice, and choices C and B place the semicolon so that it cuts the adverb away from the clause it introduces. The same pattern governs 'therefore,' 'moreover,' 'consequently,' and 'nevertheless.'
rationales.eli10: Words like 'however' sound like joining words, but they cannot actually hold two sentences together; they are commentary, not glue. The semicolon does the holding, and 'however' rides just after it with a comma trailing: stable; however, dizzy. Use only a comma and the two sentences collapse into a splice. Put the semicolon after 'however' and the commentary gets stranded away from the clause it was meant to introduce.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: 'However' is a conjunctive adverb rather than a coordinating conjunction, so it cannot join two independent clauses with a comma alone; a semicolon (or a period) must fall at the clause boundary, and a comma normally follows the adverb. questions.stem: Which revision best corrects the misplaced modifier in 'The nurse gave the discharge instructions to the patient that were printed in Spanish'?

options.text: The nurse gave the discharge instructions to the patient, which were printed in Spanish.
The nurse gave the patient the discharge instructions that were printed in Spanish.
The discharge instructions were given to the patient, that were printed in Spanish, by the nurse.
The nurse, who gave the discharge instructions, printed them in Spanish for the patient.

rationales.whyCorrect: A relative clause should sit as close as possible to the noun it modifies; in the original, 'that were printed in Spanish' follows 'patient' and momentarily seems to describe the patient. Choice B uses the indirect-object pattern ('gave the patient the instructions') so that 'instructions' stands directly before its clause, resolving the ambiguity without adding words or changing meaning. Choice A leaves the clause just as far from 'instructions' and additionally sets it off with a comma, turning a restrictive clause into a nonrestrictive one and thereby changing the meaning to imply that all the discharge instructions were printed in Spanish; choice C keeps the clause stranded and misuses 'that' in a comma-set clause; choice D changes the meaning by asserting that the nurse did the printing.
rationales.eli10: A relative clause attaches to whatever noun it sits beside. In the original it sits beside 'patient,' so the reader first hears that the patient was printed in Spanish and then has to back up and reinterpret. English lets you say 'gave the patient the instructions' just as easily as 'gave the instructions to the patient,' so reordering puts 'instructions' where the clause can reach it. Changing the seating chart usually beats adding words.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses apostrophes correctly?

options.text: It's important to check the patient's identification band before every medication.
It's important to check the patients identification band before every medication.
Its important to check the patient's identification band before every medication.
Its' important to check the patients' identification band before every medication.

rationales.whyCorrect: 'It's' is the contraction of 'it is,' while 'its' is the possessive determiner and never takes an apostrophe; because the sentence opens with 'it is,' the contraction is required, which eliminates choice C. 'Patient's' is the singular possessive marking the band as belonging to one patient, so choice B, which drops the possessive marker, is incorrect. Choice D compounds the problem: 'its'' is not a form in standard English at all.
rationales.eli10: Here is the test that never fails: read the sentence substituting 'it is.' If it still makes sense, write 'it's,' where the apostrophe stands in for the missing letter in 'is.' If 'it is' sounds wrong, you want plain 'its,' the ownership word, which takes no apostrophe for the same reason 'his' and 'hers' do not. The form 'its'' with a trailing apostrophe is never correct in any sentence.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: 'It's' is the contraction of 'it is,' while 'its' is the possessive determiner and never takes an apostrophe; because the sentence opens with 'it is,' the contraction is required, which eliminates choice C. 'Patient's' is the singular possessive marking the band as belonging to one patient, so choice B, which drops the possessive marker, is incorrect. questions.stem: Which revision best repairs the faulty parallelism in 'The instructor emphasized reading the syllabus, attending every lab, and that students should submit drafts early'?

options.text: The instructor emphasized reading the syllabus, attendance at every lab, and that drafts be submitted early.
The instructor emphasized that students read the syllabus, attending every lab, and early draft submission.
The instructor emphasized reading the syllabus, attending every lab, and submitting all drafts early.
The instructor emphasized the syllabus, every lab, and that drafts should be submitted early by students.

rationales.whyCorrect: Parallel structure requires that items joined in a series share the same grammatical form; the original pairs two gerund phrases with a noun clause. Choice C makes all three items gerund phrases ('reading,' 'attending,' 'submitting'), so each one completes the verb 'emphasized' in the same way. Choice A mixes a gerund, an abstract noun, and a clause; choice B mixes a clause, a gerund, and a noun phrase; choice D mixes two bare nouns with a clause, so each leaves the series unbalanced.
rationales.eli10: Test a list by checking whether every item can finish the opening words on its own: 'emphasized reading...,' 'emphasized attending...,' 'emphasized that students should submit...' The first two are -ing phrases and the third is a full clause, so the pattern breaks partway through and the reader has to reset. Convert the odd item to match, giving 'submitting drafts early,' and all three slot in identically. That matching is parallelism, and it is what makes lists scannable.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Parallel structure requires that items joined in a series share the same grammatical form; the original pairs two gerund phrases with a noun clause. Choice C makes all three items gerund phrases ('reading,' 'attending,' 'submitting'), so each one completes the verb 'emphasized' in the same way. Choice A mixes a gerund, an abstract noun, and a clause; choice B mixes a clause, a gerund, and a noun phrase; choice D mixes two bare nouns with a clause, so each leaves the series unbalanced.

questions.stem: What would happen to the meaning of 'The students who completed the safety module may enter the lab' if commas were placed around the clause 'who completed the safety module'?

options.text: The meaning would be unchanged, since commas around a relative clause are optional stylistic marks
The clause would become nonrestrictive, implying that all the students completed the module and all may enter
The clause would become restrictive, narrowing permission to only the subset of students who finished
The sentence would become a comma splice, since the relative clause functions as an independent clause

rationales.whyCorrect: Commas mark a relative clause as nonrestrictive, that is, as supplemental information that could be deleted without changing which people are being identified. Without commas the clause is restrictive and limits 'students' to the subset who finished the module; adding commas removes that limit, so the sentence grants entry to the whole group and merely mentions the module in passing. Choice C reverses the terms, and choice D is wrong because a relative clause is dependent and cannot form a comma splice.
rationales.eli10: Commas here mark the difference between a condition and an aside. With no commas, the clause is doing filtering work: only those particular students may enter. Add commas and the clause becomes a side note, as though everyone already qualifies and you are simply noting it. Two small marks quietly shift the rule from 'some may enter' to 'all may enter,' which is why the restrictive versus nonrestrictive distinction matters in policies and instructions.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Commas mark a relative clause as nonrestrictive, that is, as supplemental information that could be deleted without changing which people are being identified. Without commas the clause is restrictive and limits 'students' to the subset who finished the module; adding commas removes that limit, so the sentence grants entry to the whole group and merely mentions the module in passing. Choice C reverses the terms, and choice D is wrong because a relative clause is dependent and cannot form a comma splice.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines subject-verb agreement in standard written English?

options.text: The verb must match its subject in number and in person
The verb must appear immediately after the subject in every sentence
The verb must match the tense of the verb in the preceding sentence
The verb must match the gender of the noun that performs the action

rationales.whyCorrect: Agreement (concord) means the verb is inflected to match the grammatical number (singular or plural) and person (first, second, third) of its subject: "the patient reports" versus "the patients report," "I am" versus "she is." Word order and tense sequencing are separate grammatical issues, and modern English verbs carry no gender marking. Accurate agreement matters in clinical documentation because the verb form often signals whether one patient or several are being described.
rationales.eli10: Agreement is a matching rule with two settings: how many, and which person. If the subject is one third-person thing, the present-tense verb takes the -s form ("the nurse checks"); if the subject is more than one, the verb drops it ("the nurses check"). Two things the verb does not care about: gender, and distance. A long phrase can sit between the subject and the verb, and the match still has to hold across it.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Agreement (concord) means the verb is inflected to match the grammatical number (singular or plural) and person (first, second, third) of its subject: "the patient reports" versus "the patients report," "I am" versus "she is." Word order and tense sequencing are separate grammatical issues, and modern English verbs carry no gender marking. Accurate agreement matters in clinical documentation because the verb form often signals whether one patient or several are being described.

questions.stem: Which sentence shows correct subject-verb agreement?

options.text: The vital signs was recorded before the medication was given
The nursing students studies pharmacology every semester
The charts on the counter needs to be filed by the unit clerk
The patient's blood pressure remains stable after the infusion

rationales.whyCorrect: "Blood pressure" is a singular third-person subject, so it takes the singular verb "remains"; the possessive "patient's" modifies the subject but never controls the verb. The other options mismatch number: plural "vital signs" requires "were," plural "nursing students" requires "study," and plural "charts" requires "need" (the intervening phrase "on the counter" is irrelevant to the verb).
rationales.eli10: Test each sentence by swapping the subject for "it" or "they." One blood pressure is an "it," and you would say "it remains," so "remains" is right. Signs, students, and charts are all "they," and "they" takes were, study, and need. One warning about the -s ending: on a noun it usually means plural, but on a present-tense verb it means singular. That reversal is what makes "the charts needs" sound acceptable to the ear when it is not.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: "Blood pressure" is a singular third-person subject, so it takes the singular verb "remains"; the possessive "patient's" modifies the subject but never controls the verb. The other options mismatch number: plural "vital signs" requires "were," plural "nursing students" requires "study," and plural "charts" requires "need" (the intervening phrase "on the counter" is irrelevant to the verb).

questions.stem: Indefinite pronouns such as each, either, everyone, and somebody take which kind of verb?

options.text: Either a singular or a plural verb, depending on whether the writer has one person or several in mind
A plural verb, because they refer to more than one individual
A singular verb, because these pronouns are grammatically singular
A plural verb whenever a plural noun follows in an "of" phrase, as in "each of the residents"

rationales.whyCorrect: Purdue OWL lists each, each one, either, neither, everyone, everybody, anybody, anyone, nobody, somebody, someone, and no one as singular pronouns requiring singular verbs: "Each of the residents receives a flu vaccine." Grammatical number, not the collective feel of the meaning, governs the verb here, and a plural noun inside a following prepositional phrase cannot override it. (A separate issue is pronoun reference, where singular "they" is now widely accepted for the person referred to.)
rationales.eli10: Words like everyone and each sound like they cover a crowd, but grammatically they pick people out one at a time, which is exactly what "each" means. So the verb stays in the form you would use after "he" or "she": "Everyone needs a wristband." When a phrase like "of the residents" follows, cover it with your finger and read what is left: "Each ... receives." The plural noun in that phrase is bait.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Purdue OWL lists each, each one, either, neither, everyone, everybody, anybody, anyone, nobody, somebody, someone, and no one as singular pronouns requiring singular verbs: "Each of the residents receives a flu vaccine." Grammatical number, not the collective feel of the meaning, governs the verb here, and a plural noun inside a following prepositional phrase cannot override it. questions.stem: What happens to the verb when a prepositional phrase comes between the subject and the verb, as in "The box of sterile gloves ___ on the shelf"?

options.text: The verb agrees with the noun closest to it, giving "are"
The verb still agrees with the head noun "box," giving "is"
The verb may take either form, because the phrase blurs the number
The verb becomes plural because two nouns appear before it

rationales.whyCorrect: The subject of a clause is never the object of a preposition, so "of sterile gloves" is a modifier that can be mentally bracketed out; the head noun "box" governs the verb. Pulling the verb toward the nearer plural noun is a well-documented error called agreement by attraction (or proximity error). Bracketing intervening phrases is a reliable proofreading move in technical and clinical writing, where subjects are often long and heavily modified.
rationales.eli10: Cover the words "of sterile gloves" with your thumb and read what is left: "The box ___ on the shelf." One box, so "is." The gloves are just description riding along, like a label on the outside of the box, and a label does not get to choose the verb. The trick works because your ear matches the verb to whatever it heard last, and covering the phrase takes that last word away.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: The subject of a clause is never the object of a preposition, so "of sterile gloves" is a modifier that can be mentally bracketed out; the head noun "box" governs the verb. questions.stem: Which comparison of compound subjects joined by "and" versus "or" is accurate?

options.text: "And" normally creates a plural subject, while with "or" the verb agrees with the nearer subject
Both connectors join elements additively, so both produce a plural subject and a plural verb
"And" requires a singular verb, while "or" requires a plural verb
With both connectors the verb agrees with whichever subject is named first

rationales.whyCorrect: "And" joins elements additively and yields a compound plural subject: "The stethoscope and the thermometer are in the drawer." With the disjunctive connectors or and nor, standard usage applies the proximity rule, so the verb matches the nearer element: "The aides or the nurse manager is covering the shift" versus "The nurse manager or the aides are covering the shift." One exception on the "and" side: a compound naming a single entity or idea, such as "macaroni and cheese" or "research and development," takes a singular verb.
rationales.eli10: "And" works like a plus sign: one thing plus another gives more than one, so the verb goes plural. "Or" works like a choose-one sign: only one of the two will actually do the action, so the verb looks at whichever partner is standing next to it and copies that one. Because the verb depends on order with "or," reversing the two nouns can change the correct verb, and writers often park the plural one last so the sentence reads smoothly.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: "And" joins elements additively and yields a compound plural subject: "The stethoscope and the thermometer are in the drawer." questions.stem: In American usage, which statement about collective nouns such as team, staff, and committee is accurate?

options.text: They take a plural verb whenever the group named contains more than one person, so recasting the subject is unnecessary
They take a singular verb when the group acts as one unit; to stress individual action, writers recast the subject as "team members"
They take a singular verb only in the present tense; in the past tense they shift to the plural verb form
They take a plural verb whenever a phrase such as "of nurses" follows, and a singular verb otherwise

rationales.whyCorrect: American usage construes collective nouns as singular when the group functions as a single body; Purdue OWL gives "The team runs during practice." British usage allows the plural far more freely ("The team run"), which is why the plural can sound wrong to American readers. When individual members' separate actions must be emphasized, editors recommend supplying a plural head noun—"The team members meet at 0700"—rather than forcing a plural verb onto the collective noun. A following of-phrase changes nothing: "The committee of nurses meets monthly."
rationales.eli10: A collective noun is a container word: it names many people but points at one container. If the container moves as a whole, use the singular verb: the team meets, the staff decides. If you really need to show the people inside acting separately, do not fight the container word by bolting on a plural verb; open the container and name the people, as in "the team members meet." Rewriting the subject is quieter than a verb your reader will flag as an error.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: American usage construes collective nouns as singular when the group functions as a single body; Purdue OWL gives "The team runs during practice." British usage allows the plural far more freely ("The team run"), which is why the plural can sound wrong to American readers. A following of-phrase changes nothing: "The committee of nurses meets monthly."

questions.stem: What is the primary reason sentences beginning with "There" or "Here" cause agreement errors?

options.text: "There" and "Here" are pronouns that are grammatically singular in every context
"There" and "Here" are expletives, so the true subject follows the verb and is easily overlooked
"There" and "Here" turn the following verb into a linking verb that has no subject
"There" and "Here" mark the sentence as imperative, which leaves the subject unstated

rationales.whyCorrect: In "There are three consent forms on the desk," the word "there" is an expletive placeholder filling the subject slot, while the grammatical subject, "forms," is postponed until after the verb. Because English readers and writers expect the subject first, the verb is often chosen before the real subject appears, producing the very common "there's three forms." Locating the postponed subject settles the verb: "There is one form" versus "There are three forms."
rationales.eli10: "There" is a placeholder that saves a seat at the table; it is not the guest. The actual guest arrives after the verb. So before choosing is or are, read past the placeholder and count what shows up: one form arriving means "there is," three forms arriving means "there are." If the sentence still feels slippery, rewrite it without the placeholder at all: "Three consent forms sit on the desk" puts the subject back in front where the verb can see it.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: In "There are three consent forms on the desk," the word "there" is an expletive placeholder filling the subject slot, while the grammatical subject, "forms," is postponed until after the verb. Because English readers and writers expect the subject first, the verb is often chosen before the real subject appears, producing the very common "there's three forms." Locating the postponed subject settles the verb: "There is one form" versus "There are three forms."

questions.stem: A safety audit reads, "Sixty percent of the sharps containers ___ full." Which verb belongs in the blank, and why?

options.text: are, because with fractions and percentages the noun in the "of" phrase controls the verb
is, because the object of a preposition can never influence the verb of a clause
are, because a subject that contains a number larger than one takes a plural verb
is, because "percent" is the head noun of the subject and is grammatically singular

rationales.whyCorrect: With fractions, percentages, and quantifiers such as all, some, half, and most, standard usage lets the noun inside the of-phrase determine the verb, because that noun is what is actually being counted or measured: "Sixty percent of the containers are full" but "Sixty percent of the supply is gone." This is a principled exception to the general rule that an intervening prepositional phrase is ignored, which is why choices D and B, though they invoke real rules, give the wrong result here. Choice C reaches the right verb by faulty reasoning that would also produce "sixty percent of the supply are gone."
rationales.eli10: Ask yourself: sixty percent of what? If the answer is countable items, such as containers, the verb goes plural—"are full." If the answer is a single mass, such as the supply or the medication, the verb goes singular—"is gone." The percentage by itself tells you nothing about number; it is a share of something else, and that something else after "of" is the real subject matter. Note how this reverses the usual advice to ignore the "of" phrase, so it is worth memorizing as its own case.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: With fractions, percentages, and quantifiers such as all, some, half, and most, standard usage lets the noun inside the of-phrase determine the verb, because that noun is what is actually being counted or measured: "Sixty percent of the containers are full" but "Sixty percent of the supply is gone." questions.stem: Which completion is correct: "Neither the charge nurse nor the two technicians ___ available to assist with the transfer"?

options.text: was, because "neither" functions as a singular pronoun that governs the verb
was, because the first-named subject controls the verb in correlative pairs
were, because with "neither...nor" the verb agrees with the nearer subject
were, because a sentence that names more than one person takes a plural verb

rationales.whyCorrect: With the correlative conjunctions either...or and neither...nor, standard usage applies the proximity rule: the verb matches the element closest to it, here the plural "two technicians," giving "were." "Neither" is singular only when it stands alone as the subject pronoun ("Neither is available"), which is why choice A misapplies a real rule. Choice D reaches the right form by reasoning that would wrongly pluralize "Neither the technicians nor the charge nurse is available," and many style guides suggest ordering the elements so the plural comes second, since the resulting verb sounds more natural.
rationales.eli10: With neither...nor, treat the verb as nearsighted: it can only make out the subject standing right beside it. Here that neighbor is "two technicians," so the verb becomes "were." Swap the two elements and the correct verb changes with them, which is a good self-check: if flipping the order flips the verb, you are applying the rule correctly. When the result sounds awkward either way, rewrite as two clauses: "The charge nurse was not available, and neither were the technicians."
rationales.distractorAnalysis: With the correlative conjunctions either...or and neither...nor, standard usage applies the proximity rule: the verb matches the element closest to it, here the plural "two technicians," giving "were." "Neither" is singular only when it stands alone as the subject pronoun ("Neither is available"), which is why choice A misapplies a real rule. questions.stem: Which sentence uses the correct verb in the relative clause?

options.text: Maria is one of the nurses who works the night rotation on this unit
Maria is the only one of the nurses who work the night rotation on this unit
Maria is one of the nurses who work the night rotation on this unit
Maria is one of the nurse who works the night rotation on this unit

rationales.whyCorrect: In the pattern "one of the [plural noun] who," the antecedent of "who" is the plural noun "nurses," so the relative clause takes a plural verb: a group of nurses works nights, and Maria belongs to that group. The pattern reverses in choice B, because "the only one" narrows the antecedent to a single person and requires "works." Choice D also breaks number agreement inside the noun phrase ("one of the nurse"). Identifying the antecedent of the relative pronoun is the analytical step that decides the verb.
rationales.eli10: Ask who is actually working nights. In "one of the nurses who work nights," a whole group works nights and Maria is one of them, so the verb matches the group: work. Add "the only," and the group of night workers shrinks to Maria alone, so it becomes works. A quick test: move the clause to the front. "Of the nurses who work nights, Maria is one" sounds right, and it exposes which noun the who is pointing back to.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: In the pattern "one of the [plural noun] who," the antecedent of "who" is the plural noun "nurses," so the relative clause takes a plural verb: a group of nurses works nights, and Maria belongs to that group. The pattern reverses in choice B, because "the only one" narrows the antecedent to a single person and requires "works." Choice D also breaks number agreement inside the noun phrase ("one of the nurse"). Identifying the antecedent of the relative pronoun is the analytical step that decides the verb.

questions.stem: Which comparison of "the number of" and "a number of" is accurate?

options.text: Both take plural verbs, because each phrase refers to a quantity greater than one
"The number of" takes a plural verb, while "a number of" takes a singular verb
Both take singular verbs, because "number" is the head noun in each phrase
"The number of" takes a singular verb, while "a number of" takes a plural verb

rationales.whyCorrect: In "The number of readmissions has declined," the definite article points to one specific figure, so the head noun "number" governs a singular verb. In "A number of readmissions were preventable," the phrase "a number of" has been reanalyzed as a quantifier meaning "several," so the plural noun that follows controls the verb. The same split appears with related expressions such as "a variety of" and "a total of," which take plural verbs when they function as quantifiers.
rationales.eli10: "The number" names one specific figure, like the single total written at the bottom of a chart, so the verb is singular: has declined. "A number of" is not really about a figure at all; it is a roundabout way of saying "several," so the things after it are the real actors and the verb goes plural. Test it by substituting the word several: if "several readmissions were preventable" still says what you mean, use the plural verb.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: In "The number of readmissions has declined," the definite article points to one specific figure, so the head noun "number" governs a singular verb. The same split appears with related expressions such as "a variety of" and "a total of," which take plural verbs when they function as quantifiers.

questions.stem: What would result if a writer made the verb agree with the words following a linking verb, as in "The leading cause of falls ___ wet floors and poor lighting"?

options.text: No error, because a linking verb agrees with whichever noun in the sentence is plural
No error, because the predicate noun determines number in sentences built on "to be"
The plural "are" would be required, because two separate hazards are named after the verb
An agreement error, because the verb agrees with the subject "cause," so "is" is correct

rationales.whyCorrect: A linking verb agrees with its grammatical subject, not with the predicate nominative (subject complement) that follows it, so the singular subject "cause" takes "is" even though "wet floors and poor lighting" is plural. The construction is not symmetrical: the noun on the left of the verb controls agreement, however long the complement on the right becomes. Because such sentences can read awkwardly, editors often invert them—"Wet floors and poor lighting are the leading causes of falls"—which places the plural in subject position and makes the plural verb correct.
rationales.eli10: A linking verb looks like an equals sign, but grammar does not treat the two sides as interchangeable: the verb takes its number from the subject on the left, never from the complement on the right. One cause on the left means "is," no matter how many items are listed after it. If "is" followed by a long list grates on your ear, that is a signal to flip the sentence so the list becomes the subject, and then "are" is genuinely correct.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: A linking verb agrees with its grammatical subject, not with the predicate nominative (subject complement) that follows it, so the singular subject "cause" takes "is" even though "wet floors and poor lighting" is plural. The construction is not symmetrical: the noun on the left of the verb controls agreement, however long the complement on the right becomes. Because such sentences can read awkwardly, editors often invert them—"Wet floors and poor lighting are the leading causes of falls"—which places the plural in subject position and makes the plural verb correct.

questions.stem: Which term names the noun that a pronoun refers back to in a sentence?

options.text: Appositive
Antecedent
Modifier
Complement

rationales.whyCorrect: A pronoun stands in for a noun, and the noun it refers to is called its antecedent (from Latin, 'going before'). Locating the antecedent is the first step in checking agreement in number, person, and gender, and in testing whether the reference is clear. An appositive renames an adjacent noun, a modifier describes another word, and a complement completes the meaning of a verb; none of these terms names the referent of a pronoun.
rationales.eli10: A pronoun works like a nickname: if someone says 'she,' you can only follow along because a real name was mentioned earlier. That earlier name is the antecedent, a word that literally means 'the one going before.' When the nickname shows up with no name behind it, the reader has to guess, and that guessing is exactly what vague pronoun reference causes in writing.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: A pronoun stands in for a noun, and the noun it refers to is called its antecedent (from Latin, 'going before'). questions.stem: Which sentence uses the subjective (nominative) case pronoun correctly?

options.text: The instructor gave the lab results to Maria and I.
Maria and me reviewed the lab results together.
Us students reviewed the lab results with Maria.
Maria and I reviewed the lab results together.

rationales.whyCorrect: A pronoun that performs the action of the verb takes the subjective case (I, he, she, we, they). In a compound subject the case does not change, which you can confirm by dropping the other subject: 'I reviewed the lab results.' Option A places 'I' after the preposition 'to,' where the objective 'me' belongs; option B uses the objective 'me' as a subject; option C uses 'Us' where the subject pronoun 'We students' is required.
rationales.eli10: Cover the other person's name and read the sentence with the pronoun alone. 'Me reviewed the lab results' collapses immediately, so the form has to be 'I reviewed,' which gives you 'Maria and I reviewed.' The same test catches the opposite error: nobody says 'the instructor gave the results to I,' so that sentence needs 'me.'
rationales.distractorAnalysis: A pronoun that performs the action of the verb takes the subjective case (I, he, she, we, they). questions.stem: What is the key difference between the possessive pronoun 'its' and the contraction 'it's'?

options.text: 'Its' shows ownership, while 'it's' is short for 'it is' or 'it has'
'Its' is plural, while 'it's' is singular
'Its' is used for people, while 'it's' is used for objects
'Its' is a determiner used before a noun, while 'it's' is the possessive form used alone

rationales.whyCorrect: Possessive pronouns (its, hers, theirs, yours, ours) never take an apostrophe, because in English the apostrophe marks possession on nouns or signals omitted letters in a contraction. 'It's' always expands to 'it is' or 'it has,' and no possessive meaning attaches to that form. Option D reverses the roles: 'its' is indeed used before a noun, but 'it's' is never a possessive in any position.
rationales.eli10: The apostrophe in 'it's' is holding the place of letters that dropped out of 'is' or 'has.' So run the expansion out loud: 'The cell lost it is nucleus' breaks apart, which tells you the sentence needs 'its.' Possessive pronouns are already built to show ownership, so they never need an apostrophe to do that job.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Possessive pronouns (its, hers, theirs, yours, ours) never take an apostrophe, because in English the apostrophe marks possession on nouns or signals omitted letters in a contraction. 'It's' always expands to 'it is' or 'it has,' and no possessive meaning attaches to that form. Option D reverses the roles: 'its' is indeed used before a noun, but 'it's' is never a possessive in any position.

questions.stem: Standard handbooks require 'whom' rather than 'who' in the sentence 'To ___ should the report be addressed?' Why?

options.text: It functions as the object of the preposition 'to.'
It appears in a question rather than in a statement.
It refers to a person whose identity is unknown.
It appears in a sentence written in the passive voice.

rationales.whyCorrect: 'Who' is the subjective form of the interrogative and relative pronoun; 'whom' is the objective form. In this sentence the pronoun completes the preposition 'to,' so the objective case is required, as the answer 'The report should be addressed to him' confirms. Interrogative form, an unknown referent, and passive voice are all present in various correct 'who' sentences as well, so none of them determines case; only the pronoun's grammatical role inside its own clause does.
rationales.eli10: Answer the question using 'he' or 'him' and see which one survives: 'The report should be addressed to him.' If 'him' fits, the question needs 'whom,' and the shared final m makes that easy to remember; if 'he' fits, use 'who.' The question mark and the passive verb are irrelevant here because case is decided by the job the pronoun does, not by the shape of the sentence around it.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: 'Who' is the subjective form of the interrogative and relative pronoun; 'whom' is the objective form. questions.stem: Which comparison of reflexive and intensive pronouns is accurate?

options.text: A reflexive pronoun replaces a subject, while an intensive pronoun replaces an object.
A reflexive pronoun precedes the verb, while an intensive pronoun follows the verb.
A reflexive pronoun is grammatically necessary, while an intensive pronoun can be deleted.
A reflexive pronoun suits formal writing, while an intensive pronoun suits informal speech.

rationales.whyCorrect: Both types end in -self or -selves, and the difference is functional rather than formal. A reflexive pronoun serves as an object that refers back to the subject ('She injured herself'); deleting it leaves the verb without a required complement. An intensive pronoun only emphasizes a noun already present ('The instructor herself demonstrated the technique') and can be removed with no loss of grammaticality. Neither type is fixed in position, and neither is restricted to a level of formality.
rationales.eli10: Delete the -self word and see whether the sentence still stands. 'She injured' leaves the reader asking 'injured whom?', which shows the word was carrying the object slot, so it is reflexive. 'The instructor demonstrated the technique' loses nothing but emphasis when 'herself' goes, so that one was intensive. Identical word shapes, two different jobs, and the deletion test tells them apart every time.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Both types end in -self or -selves, and the difference is functional rather than formal. A reflexive pronoun serves as an object that refers back to the subject ('She injured herself'); deleting it leaves the verb without a required complement. An intensive pronoun only emphasizes a noun already present ('The instructor herself demonstrated the technique') and can be removed with no loss of grammaticality. Neither type is fixed in position, and neither is restricted to a level of formality.

questions.stem: What is the primary problem with the sentence 'When the student met with the advisor, she said the schedule was full'?

options.text: The pronoun 'she' lacks any antecedent in the sentence
The pronoun 'she' disagrees in number with its antecedent
The pronoun 'she' is in the wrong grammatical case
The pronoun 'she' has an ambiguous antecedent

rationales.whyCorrect: Ambiguous reference occurs when a pronoun could plausibly point to two or more antecedents. Here 'she' may denote either the student or the advisor, and nothing in the sentence settles the question. The pronoun is singular like both candidates and correctly takes the subjective case as the subject of 'said,' and antecedents are certainly present; the defect is that two are equally available, so the repair is to name the intended person.
rationales.eli10: Picture pointing at 'her' while two people stand side by side. Both can reasonably assume you mean them, and no rule of grammar decides it for them. That is ambiguous reference: the pronoun aims at a spot where more than one candidate is standing. The fix is not a grammar rule at all but a naming decision, such as 'the advisor said the schedule was full.'
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Ambiguous reference occurs when a pronoun could plausibly point to two or more antecedents. Here 'she' may denote either the student or the advisor, and nothing in the sentence settles the question. The pronoun is singular like both candidates and correctly takes the subjective case as the subject of 'said,' and antecedents are certainly present; the defect is that two are equally available, so the repair is to name the intended person.
